name: Munaseli Pandai
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

earlier_scan.note: Retired bookkeeping languoid on Glottolog; no references listed anywhere reachable

new_statements.quote: Stress in Alorese is marked by higher pitch. If words are uttered in isolation, such as in a wordlist, stress almost always occurs on the penultimate syllable. However, when words are uttered in fast speech, initial syllables can be reduced and the stress moves to another syllable. [...] When the phonetic schwa occurs in the antepenultimate syllable of a trisyllabic word, the stress remains on the penultimate syllable, even when the word is uttered in fast speech [...] In disyllabic words with a final consonant, free variation between penultimate and ultimate stress is observed. An example is tahak 'ripe' which can be pronounced [ˈta.hak] or [ta.ˈhak].
new_statements.citation: Sulistyono, Yunus. 2022. A history of Alorese (Austronesian): combining linguistic and oral history. PhD dissertation, Leiden University (LOT Dissertation Series 614). Utrecht: LOT.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 4 'A sketch grammar of Alorese', sec. 4.2.4.4 'Stress', pp. 90-91 (also summary sec. 4.8, p. 141)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (realised as higher pitch) falls on the penultimate syllable in citation forms; in fast speech the penult vowel of a disyllable may reduce to schwa, pushing stress to the final syllable (trisyllables keep penult stress with antepenult schwa); disyllables ending in a closed (CVC) syllable vary freely between penult and final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only for compounds: 'In compounds, stress remains on the penultimate syllable and the primary stress of the compound coincides with the word stress of the first element', e.g. onong mara [ˈɔ.nɔŋˌma.ra] 'thirsty' with secondary stress on the second member (p. 91). Nothing on secondary stress within simplex words.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) fast-speech penult reduction /ɛ/>[ə] in disyllables gives final stress ([ˈla.ra]~[lə.ˈra], [ˈma.to]~[mə.ˈto]); (ii) free variation penult~final in disyllables with a heavy final CVC syllable (tahak); (iii) lexical items with penult schwa conditioned by final stress, e.g. peku [pəˈku] 'to cut', kete [kəˈtɛ] 'that' (Table 4.20, p. 81); loan trisyllables may be clipped to disyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is explicitly about words uttered in isolation (wordlist/citation forms) versus fast connected speech; compound stress treated separately. The sketch describes the NE Pantar dialect as spoken in Pandai, Wailawar and Kabir (p. 69), i.e. the 'Pandai' half of 'Munaseli Pandai'.
new_statements.identity_note: muna1238 'Munaseli Pandai' is NOT a distinct language: it is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping languoid imported from MultiTree code adb-mun, i.e. the 'dialect' name that Ethnologue 15 (Gordon 2005) listed under the spurious Papuan language Adabe [adb] of Atauro ('Dialects: Munaseli Pandai.. No relationship to Kolana'); Glottolog marks Adabe itself spurious (Hull 1998, 2004) and ISO CR 2019-053 renamed adb to Atauran. Munaseli and Pandai are the old Alorese kingdoms/villages of north-east Pantar (Sulistyono 2022:68-69; Moro 2019:379), so the only real speech variety behind the name is Alorese, glottocode alor1247 (Austronesian, Flores-Lembata, Western Lamaholot), Pantar dialect. The quoted source describes precisely that dialect (Pandai, Wailawar, Kabir). alor1247 is ALREADY in the catalog with this same source and section, so by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this key must be aliased to alor1247, not counted as a new entity; proposed for the catalog reflects evidence quality only.

new_statements.quote: Firstly, stress may be an additional phonological factor that could play a role in contact-induced morphological simplification, as exemplified by Kusters (2003) and Molineaux (2012). Stress in Alorese is on the penultimate syllable of the stem (Klamer, 2011: 32–33). Because the suffix is unstressed, and attaches to the ultimate, unstressed, stem syllable, the suffix may be more prone to loss. [fn. 5, p. 9:] Alorese lacks phonemic geminates, while consonant lengthening only occurs in word-medial position as an effect of stress on the penultimate syllable, and when preceded by a vowel that etymologically relates to Proto-Alorese schwa *ə (Klamer, 2011: 30; Sulistyono, 2022: 75).
new_statements.citation: Dekker, Peter, Marian Klamer & Bart de Boer. 2025. Phonotactic mechanisms behind contact-induced morphological simplification in Alorese. Language Dynamics and Change 15(1): 1-?.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Sulistyono 2022 statement (penultimate); adds that the domain is the stem, i.e. subject suffixes are outside the stress window, and repeats the stress-conditioned consonant lengthening. The paper does not name a village; its source Klamer 2011 describes the Alor Kecil / Alor Besar variety, not Munaseli-Pandai specifically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem; suffixes are unstressed and do not shift stress. The medial consonant after a (historically schwa) penultimate vowel is lengthened phonetically under this stress. No stress section of its own: the paper is a modelling study of suffix loss and cites Klamer 2011 (A Short Grammar of Alorese, pp. 30, 32-33) for the placement.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the stem-based domain (suffixes unstressed) is the only detail
new_statements.identity_note: muna1238 is not a language: it is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping node for the Ethnologue-15/16 'dialect' Munaseli Pandai of the spurious Adabe [adb] (Atauro), a confusion with Alorese settlers (ISO 639-3 CR 2019-053; see the 09-17 notes). Munaseli and Pandai are villages on north-east Pantar whose speech is Alorese (alor1247), Pantar dialect. Of the two works opened, Moro 2016 is the only material actually recorded in Munaseli (Jakobus Lakka, 2016-08-06) and Pandai (Suriya Mau, 2016-08-23), plus Alor Besar; Dekker 2025 describes Alorese in general and rests on Klamer 2011, whose grammar is of the Alor Kecil variety on Alor. alor1247 is already in the catalog with Sulistyono 2022 (whose ch. 4 sketch is itself based on Pandai, Wailawar and Kabir); muna1238 should be treated as an alias of alor1247, not counted separately.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the Sulistyono 2022 statement (penultimate in isolation, final when the penult reduces to schwa, free variation in CVC-final disyllables such as tahak): Moro's Munaseli and Pandai lists, the only material collected in the two villages that the name Munaseli Pandai refers to, show exactly that pattern in the form of stress marks on the exceptions. One small difference: Sulistyono gives lara 'sun/day' as [ˈla.ra] in isolation with [ləˈra] only in fast speech, whereas Moro marks laˈra (Munaseli 'day', Alor Besar 'sun', 'day') with final stress in a wordlist elicitation.
new_statements.translation_language: IPA wordlist data with English metadata
new_statements.rule_in_words: The fieldnotes are a wordlist, not a description: there is no sentence about stress. Moro marks stress with an apostrophe before the stressed syllable on roughly 40 percent of the forms. Where marked, trisyllabic words carry the mark on the penultimate syllable (Alor Besar 93 of 93 such forms, Munaseli 19 of 21, Pandai 24 of 30, e.g. taˈmala 'star', kəˈramaŋ 'morning', kɛˈlaleiŋ 'spear'); disyllables are marked only when the stress is final, and in every such case the penultimate vowel is a schwa or reduced (ləˈrːa 'sun', məˈrːɛŋ 'night', pˈnuhuŋ 'smoke') or the final syllable is a closed CVC (taˈhak 'ripe', dəˈhɛk 'forest'); no disyllable is marked with penultimate stress (0 of 149 marked disyllables across the three villages), which is consistent with penultimate stress being the unmarked default for the roughly 60 percent of forms carrying no mark (kɔfa 'sky', fulaŋ 'moon', mala 'star').
new_statements.secondary_stress: none marked (no ˌ in any moro16 form)
new_statements.exceptions: Data-level only: final stress in disyllables whose penult is schwa/reduced or whose final syllable is CVC (ləˈrːa, taˈhak); one Pandai form flagged 'check stress' (taˈgːɛ 'sweet')
new_statements.identity_note: muna1238 is not a language: it is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping node for the Ethnologue-15/16 'dialect' Munaseli Pandai of the spurious Adabe [adb] (Atauro), a confusion with Alorese settlers (ISO 639-3 CR 2019-053; see the 09-17 notes). Munaseli and Pandai are villages on north-east Pantar whose speech is Alorese (alor1247), Pantar dialect. Of the two works opened, Moro 2016 is the only material actually recorded in Munaseli (Jakobus Lakka, 2016-08-06) and Pandai (Suriya Mau, 2016-08-23), plus Alor Besar; Dekker 2025 describes Alorese in general and rests on Klamer 2011, whose grammar is of the Alor Kecil variety on Alor. alor1247 is already in the catalog with Sulistyono 2022 (whose ch. 4 sketch is itself based on Pandai, Wailawar and Kabir); muna1238 should be treated as an alias of alor1247, not counted separately.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on the rule. Dekker, Klamer & de Boer 2025 (via Klamer 2011) and the existing Sulistyono 2022 statement both give penultimate stress; Moro's 2016 wordlists mark final stress only in disyllables with a schwa/reduced penult or a CVC final (ləˈrːa, taˈhak), which is the very exception Sulistyono describes. The one point of tension is minor: Sulistyono gives lara 'sun/day' as penultimate [ˈla.ra] in isolation and final [ləˈra] only in fast speech, while Moro's list elicitations mark laˈra with final stress in Munaseli and Alor Besar (and ləˈrːa in Munaseli and Pandai for 'sun'). Dekker 2025 also adds the stem as the domain (subject suffixes are unstressed), which Sulistyono does not state; nothing contradicts it.
